nameStory: Whale lice get their name because they're small crustaceans that live exclusively on whales, much like how regular lice live on other animals. Despite the name, they're not actually lice at all – they're more closely related to beach fleas and other amphipods you might find hopping around in seaweed!
description: Cyamus boopis is a tiny parasitic crustacean that spends its entire life attached to humpback whales. These pale, flattened creatures are about the size of a small fingernail and have strong, claw-like legs that help them grip onto their whale host's skin. They feed on the whale's skin and create small wounds, though they don't seem to seriously harm their massive hosts. You'd only encounter these unusual animals if you were lucky enough to see a whale up close during research or stranding events.

idTips.label: Host specificity
idTips.description: Found exclusively on humpback whales, never on other whale species or marine animals

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Flattened, oval body that's pale whitish or cream colored, about thumbnail-sized

idTips.label: Attachment behavior
idTips.description: Will immediately try to grab onto human hands or clothing when disturbed, using strong hook-like claws

idTips.label: Preferred locations
idTips.description: Most concentrated around the whale's genital area and where barnacles are also growing

idTips.label: Clustering pattern
idTips.description: Usually found in groups rather than individually, creating patches of infestation

habitat: You'll only find these creatures in New England waters attached to humpback whales, which migrate through our coastal waters seasonally. They're most commonly observed during whale research activities, strandings, or very rarely during close whale watching encounters. Since they live in both Atlantic and Southern Ocean waters, they travel wherever their humpback whale hosts migrate.

seasonality.spring: Present on humpback whales as they begin their northward migration into New England waters, often more visible as whales surface frequently during feeding preparation.
seasonality.summer: Most likely to be observed during peak whale watching season when humpbacks are actively feeding in New England waters and spending more time at the surface.
seasonality.fall: Still present on whales during their southward migration, though whale activity may be more dispersed as they prepare for their long journey.
seasonality.winter: Rare to observe as most humpback whales have migrated south to warmer waters for breeding, taking their whale lice with them.

funFact: These tiny hitchhikers are so loyal to their whale hosts that different whale species have their own unique species of whale lice – they're like living ID tags that help scientists identify which type of whale they're studying, even from a distance!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other whale lice species, but Cyamus boopis is specifically found on humpback whales while other Cyamus species live on different whale types. If you're looking at a humpback whale, you're looking at boopis – it's that simple!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'lice,' these creatures are actually amphipod crustaceans more closely related to sand fleas than to the lice that might bother land animals. This naming confusion often surprises people who expect them to be insects rather than tiny marine relatives of shrimp and crabs.
compareHints: Cyamus boopis differs from its close relative Cyamus ovalis primarily by its whale host preference and body proportions. While both are whale lice, boopis specifically targets humpback whales and tends to be slightly more oval-shaped, whereas ovalis may have different host preferences and a more elongated body form.
